sentences: An old tree cuts diagonally across the picture.
A cat clinging to its trunk looks down, while a second cat sitting on the ground twists its head to look back up.
In the branches above, a little flock of sparrows chatters in alarm.
This is Cats and Sparrows, known in Korean as Myojakdo, painted in ink and light colour on silk by the eighteenth-century Joseon court painter Byeon Sang-byeok.
It is a tall, narrow picture, about 94 centimetres high and 43 centimetres wide.
Byeon was born in 1730, and the year of his death is not known.
His pen name was Hwajae, and he also served as a county magistrate.
He painted cats and chickens so well that people nicknamed him "Byeon the Cat" and "Byeon the Rooster."
An old record adds that he painted more than a hundred portraits.
Now look at the climbing cat.
This grey striped cat grips the bark with its claws out and its hind legs fully stretched, bracing its whole body against the trunk.
Its back is arched and tense, yet its head turns to look down.
Follow that gaze down to the ground.
A black striped cat sits with its round front paws resting easily, neck stretched up toward its companion.
The two glances meet along a diagonal line, and that silent exchange holds the whole composition taut.
Come closer and look at the fur.
Each hair is drawn with its own stroke of a very fine brush.
The yellow eyes, the white whiskers and the pink noses are painted with the same care.
Next, look at the tree itself.
The twisted, knotted trunk is painted in wet, heavy ink with rough and confident strokes.
Precise animals against a loosely brushed tree: that contrast is what gives the picture its lively energy.
At the tips of the branches, pale green buds are opening, and six sparrows perch among them.
They seem to call out and glance at one another, as if passing on a warning.
A small drama is unfolding in a tree at the very start of spring.
There is also a wish hidden here.
In Chinese characters, the word for cat sounds like a word for a very old person, and the word for sparrow sounds like the word for magpie, a bird of joy.
So cats and sparrows became a favourite way to wish someone a long and happy life.
Halfway up the right-hand edge, the painter signed it with his pen name, Hwajae.
The painting is counted among the finest animal pictures of late Joseon, carrying on a Korean tradition that goes back to earlier masters such as Yi Am.
It belongs to the National Museum of Korea in Seoul.
Step back and see it whole.
Two cats, six sparrows and one budding tree, all holding their breath at the same moment.
Today, take a little time to watch one small living creature near you for longer than you usually would.
